title: Feature-Positive Effect
hook: The visible clue gets a voice; the missing clue has to wait for someone to ask.
counterintuition: The thing you can see may be less useful than the thing that is absent; name the feature-positive pull, then check what is missing.
tryThisNow: Pick one choice based on a visible cue. Write the absent evidence that would change your mind before you act.
keyTakeaway: The feature-positive effect makes present cues feel stronger than missing evidence. Add an explicit absence check before deciding.

breakdown.fastRead: The call log in the pension app review shows many users asking about a higher default rate. Marjorie wants to raise the default because the calls are visible. The missing cue is quieter: most users never called. The room can see the calls. She writes feature-positive on the log, adds a no-call sample check, and changes the default review only after both groups are visible.
breakdown.deepRead:
Present evidence is easier to use than absent evidence. A mark, symptom, complaint, photo, or phone call gives the mind something to hold. Absence asks for a harder question: what should be here if the claim were true?

The feature-positive effect is this tilt toward what appears. An ambulance review may overfocus on stamped forms and miss the shifts with no forms because nobody completed them. A renovation plan may chase visible cracks and miss rooms with no inspection notes. A watch retailer may treat waitlist names as demand while ignoring customers who left without signing.

Absence needs a search party.

The correction is to ask for the missing cue before the next choice moves. What evidence would be absent if the story were wrong? What group is not represented? What symptom, complaint, form, or data point did not appear? Then design the choice so absence gets a box, not an afterthought.

This matters because visible cues can be genuine and still incomplete. You should not ignore the call, crack, symptom, or form. You should stop it from becoming the whole diagnosis before the missing evidence has been invited in.
breakdown.fullRead:
The stamped form in the ambulance night-shift review shows three delayed handoffs. Cheryl, the operations lead, can see the problem in ink. What she cannot see is just as important: two crews skipped forms entirely during the busiest hour. If the review counts only stamped forms, the cleanest-looking shifts may be the least documented.

The feature-positive effect makes presence feel like proof. A visible cue is easy to count, repeat, and defend. Missing evidence is slippery. It may mean nothing happened. It may mean nobody looked. It may mean the system failed before the record began.

What should be present if your story is true?

Zhao and Pechmann's work on regulatory focus, the feature-positive effect, and message framing used anti-smoking campaigns to study how present and absent features shape response. The broader lesson travels well: people respond strongly to features that are shown, named, or framed, while absence often needs a deliberate prompt to enter judgment.

A vaccine-statistic framing case shows the same force. Beverly sees a site photo of a crowded clinic and wants the message to focus on demand. The absence is harder to see: neighborhoods with low turnout do not show up in the photo. If the campaign follows only the visible crowd, it may speak to the already-engaged and miss the people at risk.

The missing group is data too.

A viral chart fact-check makes the trap plain. Federica sees a blood-test panel that highlights one rising marker. The chart online circles the marker in red and claims a crisis. The absent evidence is the base range, the repeat test, and the people whose marker did not rise. A fact-check that follows the red circle will spread the error faster. A fact-check that asks what is missing can slow it down.

The practical correction is an absence column. Put the visible cue on the left. Put the missing cue on the right. Ask what you would expect to see if the story held, what you would expect to be absent if it were false, and which group is missing from the record. Then decide only after both sides have been named.

The limit is that absence can be ambiguous. No complaint may mean no problem, or no safe way to complain. No symptom may mean health, or a test that cannot detect the disease. The answer is not to worship absence. The answer is to make it visible enough to question.

Before the choice moves forward, give the absent evidence a place to stand. If the visible cue still carries the decision after that, use it. If the choice changes once the missing group appears, the feature was choosing for you.

examples.title: Marjorie checks the silent users
examples.scenario: A call log sits beside the pension app default-rate report in Boston at 10:05 a.m. Marjorie must decide whether caller complaints prove the default rate is too low. She marks feature-positive on the log, adds a sample of users who never called, and changes the rate review in front of the product lead.
examples.whatToDo: Compare callers with a no-call user sample before changing the default rate.
examples.whyItMatters: The calls are visible, but silent users may hold the larger pattern. The default should not answer only the people who called.

planSpec.domain: a pension app default rate applying Feature-Positive Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Cheryl counts the missing handoffs
examples.scenario: "The stamped forms show three delays," the supervisor says during an ambulance night-shift review in Leeds. Cheryl must decide whether those forms define the problem. She writes absent evidence on the stamped form, checks which crews filed nothing during peak calls, and changes the review while the duty captain watches.
examples.whatToDo: Count missing forms and stamped forms before judging the night-shift handoff problem.
examples.whyItMatters: A stamped delay is visible. A missing form may hide the worst hour because no one had time to document it.

examples.title: Irena adds the rooms with no notes
examples.scenario: The policy draft smells of dust in an architecture renovation review in Prague. Irena must decide whether visible cracks should drive the whole repair plan. She marks visible cues on the draft, asks for rooms with no inspection notes, and changes the scope only after the blank rooms are checked.
examples.whatToDo: Give uninspected rooms their own column before prioritizing the visible damage.
examples.whyItMatters: Cracks deserve attention, but absent inspection notes may hide rooms no one checked.

planSpec.domain: a architecture renovation plan applying Feature-Positive Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Signe diagnoses the empty waitlist
examples.scenario: You are looking at a floor sticker beside the watch retailer waitlist in Oslo, and every name on the list wants the same limited model. Signe must decide whether the list diagnoses total demand. She writes diagnosis on the sticker, asks staff to count walkouts who refused the list, and changes the buying plan in front of the store manager.
examples.whatToDo: Count waitlist names and walkouts before using the list as a demand diagnosis.
examples.whyItMatters: The waitlist shows visible demand. People who leave without signing may change the buying plan just as much.

planSpec.domain: a watch retailer waitlist applying Feature-Positive Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Beverly finds the missing neighborhoods
examples.scenario: It took Beverly one campaign review in Denver to see that vaccine-statistic framing kept following the most crowded clinic photo. At 5:10 p.m. in the public-health war room, Beverly, the message lead, studies the site photo that predicted demand, but the reveal was that low-turnout neighborhoods were absent from every image. Before the next message, she must decide whether the anti-smoking framing lesson means showing absence as well as presence.
examples.whatToDo: Put low-turnout neighborhoods beside crowded clinic photos before framing the vaccine message.
examples.whyItMatters: A crowd photo can prove engagement while hiding who is missing. The message needs both presence and absence.

planSpec.domain: a vaccine-statistic framing applying Feature-Positive Effect under operational pressure

examples.title: Federica's red-circle postmortem
examples.scenario: Which mattered more: the red circle or the missing baseline? Federica asks that after a viral chart fact-check in Milan reviews a blood-test panel shared online. The chart highlighted one rising marker and omitted the repeat test. She marks feature on the panel and changes the next check so every visible claim gets an absent-evidence box.
examples.whatToDo: Pair every highlighted marker with baseline, repeat-test, and missing-group checks before rating the chart.
examples.whyItMatters: The red circle makes one feature look decisive. The omitted context may decide whether the claim is true.

reviewCards.front: A visible cue is driving the room. What missing evidence should balance the cue?
reviewCards.back: Ask which absent cues would change the judgment. Missing information needs a deliberate search, not silence.
Add an explicit absence check: what should be present, and who or what is missing?
When the system would reliably have detected the cue if it were there.
No complaint can mean no problem, no safe way to complain, or no one asked.

reviewCards.front: What should sit beside a visible story?
reviewCards.back: The silent group, missing records, baseline, or absent symptom that would change the choice.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Pair every visible cue with the missing evidence that would change the decision.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a call log drives a decision, then I will sample users who never called.
If forms show a problem, then I will check which forms should exist but do not.
If one marker is highlighted, then I will ask for baseline and repeat-test evidence.
If images show engagement, then I will ask which group is absent from the images.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one visible cue you used today. Add the absent evidence that would change your decision.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a decision driven by present evidence and add an absence column.

Before the choice moves forward, give the absent evidence a place to stand.
